newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-U.K. inflation target in sight after soft PPI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.K. inflation target in sight after soft PPI.

text.p: The British government appeared to be on track to meet its inflation target when official figures released on Monday showed February factory gate prices rose at their slowest rate for over a decade.
The data supported Bank of England Governor Eddie George comments earlier in the day that the 2.5 percent inflation goal was within reach.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said factory gate, or output, prices rose by 1.3 percent in the year to February, a rate last seen in August 1986. Prices were unchanged compared with January.
Core output prices, which strip out food, drink, tobacco and petrol products, rose by just 0.5 percent in the year to February, a rate last seen in 1967.
The government swooped on the figures as proof its economic policies were working and described the data as "outstanding".
Britain now had an "unclouded outlook for prices in the high street this spring," said Angela Knight, economic secretary to the Treasury.

The central bank clearly agreed. George told reporters in Basle, Switzerland, where he was attending a meeting of central bankers, that underlying retail price inflation would hit the government's target of 2.5 percent later this year.
"We rather expect it in the course of the year," he said.
However, he cast doubt on whether inflation could stay at or below target. "The question is not whether we will reach it, but maintain it."
City economists, who had forecast a small monthly rise in factory gate prices, said the target was now in sight and there was little need for an interest rate rise.
"This is another set of excellent producer price inflation figures, suggesting that cost pressures in the economy remain remarkably subdued," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.
"The government looks increasingly likely to hit its target by the middle of the year and there is little to suggest that monetary conditions need to be tightened at the moment."
Underlying annual inflation excluding mortgage interest payments was 3.1 percent in February.
Nevertheless, Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke left interest rates unchanged at six percent when he met George last week.

Clarke, who is reluctant to raise interest rates in the run-up to the election, believes the pound's steady upward march over almost seven months will act as a restraint on growth and keep inflationary pressures at bay.
The pound has gained around 16 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August, pushing up the cost of British goods abroad.
Time is running out for a rise in interest rates before the election.
The next monetary meeting is not scheduled until April 10, by which time Prime Minister John Major is likely to have named the day for the election, which must be held by May 22 at the latest.

Financial markets expect a quarter point rate rise before the end of June, but Monday's data could enable the new government, of whichever party, to avoid an increase for a few "The market is still looking for a post-election tightening, but a string of data like today's could quickly bring even that into question," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Monday's data showed the costs of raw materials, or input prices, were still very weak, boding well for subdued factory gate prices later this year.
Input prices fell a seasonally-adjusted 0.5 percent in February and were down 6.6 percent year-on-year.
Lower oil prices combined with cheaper winter tariffs for electricity helped push input prices down, the ONS said.
